candidates.explanation: Board policy and orchestration live in the route rather than a board capability/public RSC surface. The route uses narrow trusted capability APIs and preserves an acyclic graph, but it defines no board-owned ports and does not specify single-point unexpected-error reporting. The claim that label reads run in parallel while requiring IDs from the work-item result is also internally inconsistent.

A board slice clearly owns policy and orchestration; the route uses a board read adapter, capability boundaries remain independent, authorization is layered, and unexpected failures are normalized and reported once. Credit is partial for board-owned dependencies because it deliberately omits board-language ports and directly consumes capability operation surfaces.

The board use case owns all cross-capability policy, defines narrow board ports, and uses adapters over public actor-scoped capability contracts. The RSC route invokes a board DAL entrypoint, dependencies remain acyclic, inaccessible labels are excluded without disclosure, and unexpected failures are reported once.

The board capability cleanly owns orchestration and policy, with board-language ports wired to narrow trusted server APIs. The route imports the board RSC surface, work-items and labels remain independent, authorization is enforced at each owning boundary, inaccessible labels produce a typed rejection, and unexpected failures are reported once.
